description: An application decrypts client-supplied ciphertext and returns a distinct error when PKCS7 padding is invalid, allowing byte-by-byte plaintext recovery.
A file download endpoint joins a user-supplied path without normalization. Requesting sequences like ../ can read files outside the intended directory.
A profile page renders the user's bio field through a server-side template engine. Submitting expressions in the bio changes the rendered page beyond plain text.
A networked service prints a user-supplied banner string using a printf-style call. Supplying percent directives causes memory contents to appear in the response.
Ciphertext is provided as hex. The same short key was XOR-repeated across a long English message, leaving statistical structure exploitable without the key.
Changing a numeric resource id in the URL returns another user's invoice without any additional authentication step.
An encrypted image still shows recognizable outlines because each block is transformed independently under the same key.
Smash the stack. Can you overflow the correct buffer? The program reads input with gets and a signal handler prints the flag on crash.
Control the return address. Overflow the buffer and return to the flag function in the program. Source uses gets into a small stack buffer.
Do you think you can bypass the protection and get the flag? A stack canary was added to protect against buffer overflows.
Check the admin scratchpad. After login a cookie named jwt appears. Have you heard of JWT? The site blocks the username admin at the form but trusts the token role.
A menu-driven program allocates two heap buffers next to each other. Overflowing the input buffer overwrites a neighbouring safe variable used as a flag gate.
This website lets you read files after login. The read endpoint checks a MAC over the filename. Flag is at /etc/flag.txt. Hints mention cheese length and implementing MAC.
The ciphertext looks like English letters with shifted alphabet positions. Frequency analysis should recover the plaintext motto.
You are given a USB disk image. Recover a deleted document from unallocated space. Standard forensic imaging formats apply.
Reverse engineer this crackme. Enter the correct serial for your name to print the flag. The check is entirely local in the binary.
Try start. Nested password-protected archives lead through a chain of files; one archive comment channel encodes bits of the final password.
A page greets you by name using a server-side template. Special template syntax in the name field evaluates expressions on the server.
RSA encryption with a very small public exponent and no padding. The message is short enough that modular exponentiation does not wrap.
Investigate this packet capture. Extract the file that was transferred over HTTP and open it for the flag.
The program prints your input with printf. Using format specifiers you can leak stack addresses and write arbitrary values.
Find where this photo was taken. The image may still contain location metadata from the camera.
A login form builds SQL with string concatenation. Entering a quote changes the error message. Can you log in as admin without the password?
The flag was XOR-encrypted with a single repeated byte. Ciphertext is provided as hex. Recover the key and plaintext.
The binary checks a password against an obfuscated string built at runtime. Recover the expected password by reversing the transform.
Someone forgot to strip metadata from this JPEG. The photographer and camera model are still embedded in the file.
NX is enabled so shellcode will not run on the stack. There is a win function already in the binary. Overflow the buffer and return to it.
Smash the stack. Can you overflow the correct buffer? Input is read with gets; a SIGSEGV handler may print the flag.
Control the return address. Overflow a small stack buffer and redirect execution to a win function already present in the binary.
A stack canary protects against buffer overflows. Leak or brute the canary, then overwrite the return address.
Two heap chunks sit next to each other. Overflowing the first overwrites a neighbouring safe variable used as a gate.
The program prints user input with printf. Using format specifiers, leak addresses and overwrite a GOT entry.
NX is enabled so stack shellcode will not run. Divert control flow into libc to obtain a shell.
Build a ROP chain from gadgets in the binary to call system with /bin/sh. ASLR is off for this instance.
After login a cookie named jwt appears. The site blocks username admin at the form but trusts the token role field.
The login form concatenates username into SQL. A single quote changes the error. Log in as admin without the password.
A greeting page renders your name through a server-side template engine. Template expressions in the name field are evaluated.
A page loads files via a path query parameter. Directory traversal may reach /etc/passwd or the application source.
A search box reflects input without encoding. Steal an admin session cookie via a crafted payload the bot will visit.
Front-end and back-end disagree on Content-Length versus Transfer-Encoding. A crafted request can desync and smuggle a second request.
The ciphertext looks like English with shifted alphabet positions. Frequency analysis should recover the motto.
The flag was XOR-encrypted with one repeated byte. Ciphertext is hex. Recover the key and plaintext.
A long ciphertext was produced by XORing plaintext with a short repeating key. Kasiski-style analysis reveals the key length.
Textbook RSA with public exponent three and no padding. The message is short enough that cubing does not wrap the modulus.
The same message was encrypted under two RSA public keys that share a modulus. Recover the plaintext without factoring.
Two ECDSA signatures were produced with the same ephemeral nonce. Recover the private key from the pair of signatures.
Investigate this packet capture. Extract the file transferred over HTTP and open it for the flag.
